ch: God calls Abraham and covenants with his family — the people through whom the Messiah comes and the Scriptures are given.
After the exile the Temple is rebuilt; synagogues, scribes, Pharisees and Sadducees shape the world Jesus is born into.
The life, death and resurrection of Jesus, and the church he builds on the apostles — the trunk of everything on this page.
After the Temple's destruction, Judaism is rebuilt around Torah, synagogue and the rabbis — Christianity's elder sibling, not its child.
From Jerusalem to the whole empire in three centuries — through persecution, the writing of the New Testament, and the church fathers.

Constantine and Licinius grant Christians the freedom to worship, ending three centuries of intermittent persecution. Within a dozen years an emperor is summoning the church's first general council — the faith has moved from the catacombs to the council chamber, for good and for ill.
The councils of Nicaea and Constantinople confess Christ as fully God — the creed nearly every church on this page still holds.

Chalcedon confessed Christ in two natures and one person, and its canons ranked the great sees. Egypt, Syria and Armenia heard 'two natures' as dividing Christ himself and could not sign — so the church came out of 451 as two families instead of one.
Rome, Constantinople, Alexandria, Antioch and Jerusalem — the five great sees of the ancient church, from which the oldest branches descend.

Teachers like Valentinus and Basilides offered salvation by secret knowledge, with the world's Maker a lesser god and Christ's flesh an appearance. Answering them pressed the church to say out loud what it had always assumed: one God who made matter and called it good, one Christ truly in the flesh, and a faith taught publicly, not whispered.

Marcion held that the God of Israel and the Father of Jesus were two different Gods, threw out the Old Testament entirely, and kept an edited Luke with ten of Paul's letters — the first list anyone is known to have drawn up. Rome expelled him and gave his money back. His truncated Bible is a large part of why the church set about naming its own.

A prophetic renewal out of Phrygia — Montanus with the prophetesses Prisca and Maximilla — calling for rigorous fasting, readiness for martyrdom and fresh utterance of the Spirit. It won Tertullian, the age's sharpest Latin mind, and raised a question the church has never finally closed: how does living prophecy sit under settled Scripture?

Arius of Alexandria taught that the Son was the Father's first and highest creature — exalted, but not God as the Father is God. Nicaea condemned it in 325, yet for most of that century it held the imperial court, and the Germanic peoples evangelized in that window — Goths, Vandals, Burgundians, Lombards — carried it into the kingdoms they built on Rome's ruins. It outlived the empire by two centuries and then died with those kingdoms: the last Arian rulers conformed in the 580s to 660s, and by the late 7th century it was gone. The Nicene Creed exists because of this argument.

When persecution ended, North African rigorists refused the ministry of bishops who had handed over the Scriptures under threat — a church of the pure, or none at all. Against them Augustine argued that a sacrament's worth rests on Christ, not on the minister's record. The Donatist church outnumbered his in Africa for a century.

The council deposed Nestorius over how to name Christ's two natures in one person. The churches of the Persian Empire — outside Roman politics, and reading the Greek terms differently — never accepted it. The first lasting division in Christian history.
The church of the Persian Empire, out of communion after the Council of Ephesus; often called 'Nestorian', though it rejects the label. Its missionaries reached China by 635.
India's ancient Christians trace their founding to the apostle Thomas; for centuries they worshipped in fellowship with the Church of the East.
The continuing Church of the East, its patriarchate today in Erbil, Iraq — a small, ancient communion scattered by a century of persecution.
A 1968 division within the Assyrian church, largely over the calendar; based in Baghdad.

The churches that could not accept Chalcedon's wording about Christ's two natures — 'miaphysite', confessing one united divine-human nature. Their objection was never only theological: Chalcedon's canons also raised Constantinople to rank beside Rome, and Alexandria and Antioch — the sees being demoted — heard the imperial capital legislating over churches older than itself.
Egypt's ancient church, tracing its founding to Mark the evangelist in Alexandria; the mother church of African Christianity.
The church of Antioch's Syriac-speaking heartland, still praying in a dialect of the language Jesus spoke.
Armenia became the first Christian kingdom in 301; its church later stood with the non-Chalcedonian family.
Founded under Frumentius and the kings of Aksum; daughter of the Coptic church until full independence in 1959, and Africa's largest ancient church.
Became a self-governing church after Eritrean independence, with the Coptic pope's blessing.

Gathered at Mattancherry, the St Thomas Christians swore never again to submit to Portuguese bishops. The oath split India’s ancient church: a minority stayed with Rome, while most sought bishops from the Syriac Orthodox instead.
After the Coonan Cross Oath against Portuguese control, many St Thomas Christians aligned with the Syriac Orthodox — India's Oriental Orthodox family.

Legates from Rome and the patriarch of Constantinople excommunicated one another in 1054 — the formal rupture in a drift already centuries old, over papal authority, a clause added to the creed, and two halves of Christendom that had stopped listening to each other. East and West have been separate communions ever since.
The Greek East after the schism: the Chalcedonian churches of Constantinople and the Slavic lands, holding the seven councils, governed as a communion of equals rather than under one see.
Constantinople's patriarch, 'first among equals' of the Orthodox world — a seniority of honour, not a papacy.
Georgia's national church, evangelized by St Nino in the 320s; its independence was suppressed under Russia and restored in 1917.

The Chalcedonian half of the ancient patriarchate of Antioch — the city where believers were first called Christians. Arabic-speaking, seated today in Damascus, and with a large diaspora in the Americas that has drawn in many Western converts.
The first Slavic national church to win its own patriarchate, in 927 — fruit of the mission of Cyril and Methodius's disciples.
Prince Vladimir's baptism of Kyiv in 988 planted the faith among the Rus; Moscow became a patriarchate in 1589 — the largest Orthodox church.
St Sava won self-government for the Serbian church in 1219; it remains at the heart of Serbian identity.

Patriarch Nikon corrected Russian service books and even the sign of the cross against contemporary Greek models. To many believers the changes touched holiness itself rather than detail; the councils of 1666–67 anathematized all who refused, and Russian Orthodoxy tore in two.
Russians who refused Patriarch Nikon's revisions to the service books, and were fiercely persecuted for keeping the old rites.
Independent after the Greek War of Independence — the national church of the modern Greek state.
United and self-governing from 1872, a patriarchate from 1925 — today the second-largest Orthodox church.
Recognized by Constantinople in 2019 as Ukraine's self-governing church — a recognition Moscow rejects; the wound is still open.
The Latin West under the bishop of Rome — through the medieval centuries, the Counter-Reformation, and two Vatican councils, the largest body in Christianity.
Twenty-three Eastern churches in full communion with Rome while keeping their own rites — Maronite, Chaldean, Ukrainian Greek Catholic, Melkite, Syro-Malabar and more.

Rome's own reforming council answered the Reformation point by point — defining canon, tradition, justification and the sacraments, and ending abuses that had helped provoke the split. It also set the divide in stone: the two Wests were now confessionally, not merely politically, apart. Its settlement shaped Catholic life for four centuries.

Rome opened the windows: the liturgy in the people's own languages, Scripture put into every hand, and a warmer word for other Christians. Most Catholics received it gladly — a minority held that the council had given away exactly what Trent was called to defend.

Benedict's Rule — prayer and work, under an abbot, in one place for life — became the pattern for Western monasticism. For centuries the monasteries were the West's schools, hospitals, farms and copyists: nearly every ancient book we still have survived because a monk wrote it out again.

A new kind of order that owned nothing and stayed nowhere: Francis's brothers preaching poverty in the growing towns, Dominic's preaching against heresy with study as their weapon. Between them they put the church back on the road — and gave the medieval universities their finest teachers, Aquinas among them.

Ignatius of Loyola's company, approved in 1540 under a special vow of obedience to the pope — schoolmasters, spiritual directors and missionaries who went wherever they were sent. They were the sharp edge of the Catholic Reformation, and carried it to India, Japan, China and the Americas.

The council defined papal infallibility: the pope, teaching solemnly from his office on faith and morals, is preserved from error. It settled centuries of argument about where authority finally rests in the Western church — and a body of German, Swiss and Dutch scholars who could not accept it walked out.

Those who rejected the 1870 definition, joined by the long-independent see of Utrecht, formed their own communion in 1889 — Catholic in worship and orders, without the papacy. Small, and in full communion with the Anglicans since 1931.
Peter Waldo of Lyon gave away his wealth and sent out lay preachers with a vernacular Bible — persecuted for centuries, and still alive in Italy today.
John Wycliffe's circle translated the first complete English Bible and questioned the church's wealth and hierarchy — 'the morning star of the Reformation'.
The Bohemian reformer, burned at Constance in 1415; his followers defied crusades and kept a reformed church in Bohemia a century before Luther.
The Unity of the Brethren, renewed at Herrnhut in 1727 — pioneers of Protestant world mission whose warmth helped light John Wesley's heart.
Luther's Ninety-five Theses open a recovery of the gospel — salvation by grace alone through faith alone, and the Bible in the people's tongue. Every Protestant branch below descends from here.

Ordered to recant before the emperor, Luther refused and was declared an outlaw. Sheltered by his own prince, he spent the exile translating the New Testament into German — and the princes who protected him began reforming the churches of their own territories.

Philipp Spener's Pia Desideria asked what a state church full of baptized strangers was for, and answered with small groups over the Bible, a living new birth, and lay people doing the work of ministry. Halle sent out the first Protestant missionaries. Nearly every warm-hearted movement below — Moravian, Methodist, Brethren, and the evangelicalism that came of them — drinks from this well.
Zwingli in Zurich and Calvin in Geneva build the Reformation's second great stream — God's sovereignty, covenant, and churches governed by elders.
France's Reformed church, organized in 1559 and refined by fire — massacre and exile scattered Huguenot believers (and their skills) across the world, including the Cape.
The Reformed church of the Netherlands, whose Synod of Dort (1618–19) gave the classic five points of Calvinism.

Called to settle whether grace is finally God's choice or man's, the synod answered Arminius's followers point for point — the five heads of doctrine later remembered as the five points of Calvinism. It also ordered the Dutch Bible that shaped the language. The losing side was deposed and exiled, and Reformed Christianity has argued along this line ever since.

Followers of Jacobus Arminius who petitioned in 1610 for a gentler reading of election — grace that can be resisted, an atonement offered to all. Condemned at Dort and driven out, they organized as their own church in 1619. Their theology outlived their numbers: Wesley preached it, and most of the Methodist and Pentecostal world holds it still.
Planted at the Cape with Van Riebeeck's settlement (first congregation 1665) — for three centuries the largest church of the Afrikaans world.
John Knox brings Geneva's reformation home; Scotland's kirk, governed by elders and courts, becomes the mother of world Presbyterianism.
English Puritans who gathered self-governing congregations of the converted; the Mayflower Pilgrims carried the pattern to New England in 1620.

Parliament declared Henry VIII supreme head of the church in England, settling a king's marriage dispute by cutting a whole realm loose from Rome. It began as a question of jurisdiction, not doctrine — but the door it opened is the one Cranmer's Prayer Book and Elizabeth's settlement walked through.
Henry VIII's break with Rome became, under Cranmer and Elizabeth, a reformed church with an ancient shape — Bible, Prayer Book, bishops.

Elizabeth's Act of Uniformity fixed one Prayer Book and one church for England, framed broadly enough to hold most of the nation. Puritans who wanted the reform carried further stayed and pressed for it; those who gave up on the established church left it altogether — and English free-church Christianity begins there.
Those who despaired of reforming the established church from within and left it — the seedbed of Baptists, Congregationalists and Quakers.
American Anglicans reorganized after independence — the first self-governing church of what became the Anglican Communion.

Newman, Keble and Pusey argued that the Church of England was no creature of Parliament but a branch of the ancient catholic church, and set about recovering what went with that — the sacraments, the fathers, the religious orders, ceremony. It remade Anglican worship, sent slum priests into the cities, and lost Newman himself to Rome.
The worldwide family of Anglican churches, meeting since the first Lambeth Conference of 1867; its centre of gravity is now the global South.
Zurich radicals who baptized one another as believing adults in 1525 — the 'radical reformation' of gathered, non-violent, suffering churches.
Anabaptists who hold all goods in common, after Acts 2 — still living communally on the North American plains.
Named for Menno Simons, the Dutch priest who gathered the scattered Anabaptists into enduring peaceful churches.
Jakob Ammann's stricter Mennonites — plain dress, plain living, and community set apart from the modern world.
German Pietists baptized in the river Eder in 1708, blending Anabaptist and Pietist streams — ancestors of the Church of the Brethren.
George Fox's movement of the Inward Light — silent waiting on God, plain speech, and early witness against slavery.
John Smyth's exiled English congregation embraced believers' baptism in Amsterdam in 1609; General (free-will) and Particular (Reformed) streams soon grew.
London's Calvinistic Baptists, whose 1689 confession still anchors Reformed Baptist churches — the stream of Bunyan, Carey and Spurgeon.
Formed in 1845 in a split over slavery (a beginning it has formally repented of); today the largest Protestant denomination in the United States.
The great Black Baptist conventions, gathered in 1895 — the churches that carried, and led, the American civil-rights movement.
John Wesley's heart 'strangely warmed' in 1738; with Charles's hymns and field preaching, a revival society inside the Church of England became a worldwide church.
At the Christmas Conference in Baltimore, American Methodism became a church of its own — and grew faster than the frontier.
Richard Allen, once enslaved, led Black Methodists out of segregated pews into the first Black-led denomination in America.
William and Catherine Booth took Wesley's gospel to London's poorest streets — soup, soap and salvation, under a flag instead of a steeple.
A. B. Simpson's missionary movement around the 'fourfold gospel' — Christ our Saviour, Sanctifier, Healer and Coming King.
'Christians only, no creed but Christ' — Barton Stone's and the Campbells' movements united in 1832 to restore simple New Testament church life.
Believers in Dublin began breaking bread with no clergy at all; J. N. Darby's teaching here shaped dispensationalism and much of evangelical prophecy belief.
Organized in 1863 with Ellen White among its founders — Sabbath-keeping, health-minded, and now one of the most widespread Protestant bodies on earth.
Speaking in tongues at Topeka (1901) and then William Seymour's multiracial revival on Azusa Street (1906) — the spring from which world Pentecostalism flows.
Bishop C. H. Mason's church embraced the Azusa revival in 1907 — the largest Pentecostal denomination in the United States.
An Appalachian holiness fellowship (1886) that received Pentecost after Azusa — now a global movement.
Organized at Hot Springs, Arkansas in 1914; today the largest Pentecostal family in the world.
Aimee Semple McPherson's Angelus Temple and its worldwide offspring — Jesus the Saviour, Baptizer, Healer and Coming King.
Azusa's fire reached Johannesburg with John G. Lake in 1908 — South Africa's first Pentecostal church, and the AFM remains one of its largest.
Chuck Smith welcomed the barefoot Jesus People of the California coast — verse-by-verse teaching and casual worship that reshaped evangelicalism.
John Wimber's 'signs and wonders' churches — intimate worship and everyday ministry in the Spirit's power; its songbook went round the world.
Thousands of churches founded by African leaders — Ethiopian, Zionist and Apostolic streams — now numbering tens of millions across the continent.
Engenas Lekganyane's church, headquartered at Moria in Limpopo — its Easter gathering is among the largest Christian assemblies anywhere.

Isaiah Shembe's church, gathered at Ekuphakameni in KwaZulu-Natal — Sabbath-keeping, barefoot before God, and worshipping in sacred dance. One of the largest African-Initiated churches in South Africa, and among the most distinctly Zulu in its forms.

The 'owners of prayer' — Yoruba prayer movements born in the influenza years and the revival of 1930: the Cherubim and Seraphim, the Church of the Lord, the Christ Apostolic Church. Healing, prophecy and fasting instead of the mission hospital, and the seedbed of Nigeria's later Pentecostal explosion.
Founded in Lagos in 1952, now planting churches on every continent — a flagship of Nigeria's extraordinary missionary energy.
New England Congregationalism's liberal wing set aside the Trinity; merged with the Universalists in 1961 into a creedless association.
John Thomas's Bible-study movement, rejecting the Trinity while awaiting Christ's literal kingdom.
Charles Taze Russell's Bible Students, renamed in 1931 — door-to-door witness, a distinct New World Translation, and a non-Trinitarian theology.
Mary Baker Eddy's teaching that sickness is an error of mind to be healed by prayer — a 19th-century 'metaphysical' reading of Christianity.
otd: At a small Bible school in Topeka, Kansas, a student named Agnes Ozman asks for prayer and begins to speak in an unknown tongue. Charles Parham's students had gone to Acts to ask what the baptism in the Spirit looked like; the answer they believed they found here would be carried to Azusa Street five years later, and from there to the world.
Basil the Great and Gregory of Nazianzus

The two friends among the Cappadocian Fathers, commemorated together. Between them they defended the full deity of the Spirit, gave the Nicene faith its settled language, and left the East a pattern of pastoral care and monastic life it has never abandoned.
The bull Decet Romanum Pontificem formally excommunicates Martin Luther after he refused to recant — cutting the reformer loose from the Roman Church. See the vault's [[Protestant Reformation]] note.

Jim Elliot, Nate Saint, Ed McCully, Peter Fleming and Roger Youderian are speared on a river beach by the Waodani people they had come to reach. Elliot's journal had already answered: 'He is no fool who gives what he cannot keep to gain what he cannot lose.'
Commemoration of the father of Christian monasticism, who gave away his goods and withdrew to the Egyptian desert; his Life by Athanasius shaped the monastic movement.
The first believers' baptism at Zurich

In a house near the Zurich fish market, Conrad Grebel baptizes George Blaurock at his own request, and Blaurock baptizes the rest — grown men and women confessing faith and being baptized on it. The city council had forbidden exactly this the day before. The Anabaptist movement, and with it every free church that gathers on believers' baptism, begins in that room.

The monk sent from Frankish lands into Denmark and Sweden, who built the first churches of Scandinavia and saw most of his work undone in his lifetime. What he planted took root a century later — a reminder that a missionary's harvest is not always his own to see.

Twenty-six Christians — Franciscan missionaries, Jesuits and Japanese laymen, the youngest a boy of twelve — are crucified on a hill above Nagasaki as Japan closes against the faith. The church went underground for two and a half centuries and was found still praying when the country reopened.
Cyril and Methodius, apostles to the Slavs
The brother-missionaries who evangelised the Slavic peoples and devised the alphabet that carried Scripture and liturgy into their tongue.

Commemoration of the reformer on the day he died at Eisleben, the town where he was born. Lutheran and Anglican calendars keep the day — not for the man's temper or his worst pages, but for the recovery he was given to make: that a sinner is justified by grace through faith, and that the Bible belongs in the people's own tongue. See the vault's [[Martin Luther]] note.

Bishop of Smyrna and a hearer of the apostle John, burned in the stadium as an old man. Told to curse Christ and go free, he answered that he had served him eighty-six years and been done no wrong by him. The account of his death is the church's earliest surviving martyrdom story after the New Testament.
Emperor Theodosius I makes Nicene Christianity the official religion of the Roman Empire — a decisive turn from persecuted faith to established church.

Wales's own bishop and patron, remembered for a monastic rule so plain his monks pulled the ploughs themselves. His reported last words to them were to be joyful, keep the faith, and do the little things they had seen him do.

A young noblewoman of Carthage and the slave woman imprisoned with her, killed in the arena for refusing to sacrifice to the emperor. Perpetua's prison diary — one of the earliest surviving writings by a Christian woman — records her father begging her to recant and her plain refusal to call herself anything but a Christian.

Commemoration of the Dominican 'Angelic Doctor' on the day of his death, en route to the Council of Lyon — the older Western calendar kept his feast this day. His Summa Theologiae remains the most influential system of theology the medieval church produced.
British and Foreign Bible Society founded
Founded in London to put the Scriptures — 'without note or comment' — into every language and every hand, the Bible Society opens the great century of Bible translation and distribution.

Commemoration of the monk-pope who sent Augustine's mission to the English and shaped the worship, pastoral care and chant of the Western church. Kept this day — his death — in the older calendars; the modern Roman feast is 3 September.
Commemoration of the fifth-century bishop who, once a captive slave in Ireland, returned to evangelise the island. Traditionally kept on the day of his death.

Under Mary's restoration of Rome, the archbishop who gave England the Book of Common Prayer had signed recantations in prison. Brought out to be burned anyway, he took them back in front of the crowd — and in the fire held out first the hand that had signed them. His Prayer Book still shapes how English-speaking Christians pray.

The archbishop of San Salvador is shot at the altar, a day after publicly ordering the country's soldiers to stop killing their own people. A cautious churchman when appointed, he had been changed by burying the poor of his own diocese — and the church he was killed in front of has since named him a martyr.
The Slave Trade Act receives royal assent
On the feast of the Annunciation, Britain abolishes the transatlantic slave trade — the fruit of the twenty-year parliamentary campaign of William Wilberforce and the Clapham evangelicals.

Around three hundred preachers gather in an old opera house at Hot Springs, Arkansas, to bring order to a revival that had spread faster than anyone could shepherd it — agreeing on doctrine, missions and ministerial credentials without surrendering local church independence. The fellowship they formed is now the largest Pentecostal family in the world.

The rector of a comfortable Episcopal church in Van Nuys, California, tells his congregation from the pulpit that he has been baptized in the Spirit and has spoken in tongues. He resigned the same day — and the story went national. What had been a Pentecostal movement outside the historic churches was now loose inside them.
The conclave elects Urban VI; within months the French cardinals repudiate him and elect a rival, leaving Western Christendom with two — later three — competing popes for nearly forty years.
In a Los Angeles mission on Azusa Street, a revival under William Seymour ignites in April 1906 — widely reckoned the birthplace of the worldwide Pentecostal movement.

The theologian of the Confessing Church is hanged for his part in the resistance against Hitler, weeks before the camp's liberation. 'When Christ calls a man,' he had written, 'he bids him come and die.'
Luther before the Diet of Worms
Ordered to recant, Luther refused unless convinced by Scripture and plain reason — the words later summarised as 'Here I stand; I can do no other.' See the vault's [[Protestant Reformation]] note.
Commemoration of the archbishop and father of scholastic theology — 'faith seeking understanding' — whose Cur Deus Homo reshaped how the West speaks of the atonement.
Commemoration of the soldier-martyr of the Diocletian persecution, later patron of England and of many lands East and West.
The missionary bishop of Prague is martyred among the pagan Prussians on the Baltic frontier — an early witness of the gospel's push into northern Europe.
Commemoration of the Dominican tertiary of Siena, counsellor of popes, who pressed Gregory XI to return the papacy from Avignon to Rome and left a body of letters and the Dialogue.

By the traditional reckoning the 'Authorized Version' is published in London — the translation whose cadences would shape English-speaking faith and language for four centuries. The exact day is uncertain; early May 1611 is the customary date.

The first ecumenical council, convened by Constantine, meets to answer the Arian controversy and gives the church the original Nicene Creed. See the vault's [[Constantine]] and [[Athanasius of Alexandria]] notes.
At a meeting in Aldersgate Street, London, John Wesley felt his heart 'strangely warmed' and trusted Christ alone for salvation — a turning point for the Evangelical Revival.
Commemoration of the monk of Jarrow, 'father of English history,' who died on the eve of Ascension 735 still dictating his English translation of John's Gospel.
Commemoration of the reluctant missionary Gregory the Great sent to Kent in 597 — first archbishop of Canterbury, whose mission planted the English church.

In May 1908 the Pentecostal work John G. Lake and Thomas Hezmalhalch had begun in Doornfontein, Johannesburg gives itself a constitution and an executive — South Africa's first Pentecostal church. It began as a mixed congregation, conformed to segregation under pressure, and only reunited across those lines in 1996.
The Byzantine capital falls to the Ottoman Turks, ending the thousand-year Eastern Roman Empire and turning the great church of Hagia Sophia into a mosque — a watershed for Eastern Christianity.
The Confessing Church synod at Barmen adopts its declaration against the Nazi-aligned 'German Christians' — the church belongs to Christ alone and hears no other voice. Drafted chiefly by Karl Barth.

A philosopher who kept his cloak after conversion because he believed he had finally found the true philosophy. He wrote the first great defences of the faith to a hostile empire, left the earliest description we have of an ordinary Sunday service, and was beheaded in Rome for refusing to sacrifice.
Commemoration of Charles Lwanga and his companions, pages of the Buganda court burned at Namugongo for refusing to renounce Christ — seed of one of Africa's fastest-growing churches.
Commemoration of the English monk who evangelised the German lands — felling the pagan Oak of Thor — and was martyred at Dokkum with his companions.
Commemoration of the Irish abbot whose island monastery of Iona became the base for the evangelisation of Scotland and the north of England.

The World Missionary Conference opens in Edinburgh — some 1,200 delegates surveying the evangelisation of the world in their generation; commonly counted the birthplace of the modern ecumenical movement.
Pope Leo X issues the bull Exsurge Domine, condemning 41 of Luther's propositions and giving him sixty days to recant — the formal opening of Rome's case against the Reformation.
The third ecumenical council affirms that Mary bore one who is truly God (Theotokos) and condemns Nestorius — safeguarding the unity of Christ's person.
The foundational Lutheran statement of faith is read before Emperor Charles V at the Diet of Augsburg — the confessional charter of the Reformation churches.
At Brighton, James Hudson Taylor founds the China Inland Mission — interdenominational, inland-focused, its missionaries wearing Chinese dress — the pattern for a century of 'faith missions.'

Bishop in Gaul, taught by Polycarp who was taught by John — a living chain back to the apostles, and he knew it. Against the Gnostics he argued that the church's faith was public, handed down and the same everywhere, and he is the first writer we have who treats the four gospels as a settled four.
The assembly of divines meets in Westminster Abbey to reform the English church; its Confession and catechisms remain the doctrinal standard of Presbyterian churches worldwide.
The Czech reformer is burned at the Council of Constance despite a promised safe-conduct — a Protestant forerunner a century before Luther.
On the same date, 120 years after Hus, the Lord Chancellor Thomas More is beheaded for refusing to accept Henry VIII as head of the church in England — 'the king's good servant, but God's first.'
At Enfield, Connecticut, Jonathan Edwards preaches 'Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God' — the Great Awakening's most famous sermon, pleading with the unconverted to flee to Christ.
The first Protestant mission to South Africa

The Moravian Georg Schmidt lands at the Cape and begins work among the Khoikhoi at Baviaanskloof, later Genadendal ('vale of grace'). Expelled after seven years, his work outlived him: when missionaries returned fifty years on, his converts were still reading the Testament he left.
Commemoration of the father of Western monasticism, whose Rule — ordering a life of prayer and work, 'ora et labora' — shaped European Christianity for a millennium.

After a five-week siege the armies of the First Crusade break into Jerusalem and massacre much of the city — Muslim, Jewish and Eastern Christian alike. Preached as a pilgrimage in arms, it left a wound between the faiths, and between the Latin West and the Christian East, that has never fully closed.
Legates of the pope and the patriarch of Constantinople exchange mutual excommunications, the symbolic break between the Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches.

On the anniversary of the Great Schism, the International Congress on World Evangelization opens at Lausanne — some 2,400 evangelicals from 150 nations; its Covenant, drafted under John Stott, weds evangelism and social responsibility.

The First Vatican Council promulgates Pastor Aeternus: the pope, teaching solemnly on faith and morals from his office, is preserved from error. Most Catholics received it; a body of German, Swiss and Dutch clergy and scholars could not, and left to form the Old Catholic churches.
Commemorated on the feast of Prince Vladimir: his people baptised in the Dnieper, turning the Rus toward Byzantine Christianity — the fountainhead of Russian and Ukrainian Orthodoxy.
Commemoration of the deacon of Rome who, ordered to hand over the church's treasure, presented the poor — and was martyred in the Valerian persecution.
Commemoration of the abbot of Clairvaux, the dominant churchman of his century — mystic, preacher and hymn-writer ('Jesus, the very thought of thee') — whose Cistercians renewed European monasticism.
A wave of mob and state violence against French Protestants (Huguenots) begins in Paris and spreads across France — thousands killed. A grievous day the feast now shares.
Commemoration of the bishop of Hippo, the greatest theologian of the Latin church — Confessions, City of God, and the doctrine of grace against Pelagius. See the vault's [[Augustine of Hippo]] note.
The Slavery Abolition Act receives royal assent
Slavery is abolished across most of the British Empire — a month after William Wilberforce died, having lived just long enough to hear the bill would pass.

Commemoration of the tinker-preacher of Bedford, imprisoned twelve years for unlicensed preaching, whose Pilgrim's Progress became the most-read book in English after the Bible. He died on 31 August 1688; the Church of England keeps his day on the 30th.

Duke William of Aquitaine signs the charter founding the abbey of Cluny — free of lay control, answerable to Rome alone — the springboard of the great medieval reform of the church. The charter is dated 11 September; the year is given as 909 or 910.
Commemoration of the 'golden-mouthed' preacher and archbishop of Constantinople, greatest of the Greek Fathers as an expositor of Scripture, exiled for his plain rebukes of the powerful.

The empire ends thirty years of religious war by letting each prince settle the confession of his own territory — cuius regio, eius religio. It bought peace and cost conscience: subjects who dissented could emigrate, and no one but Lutherans and Catholics was covered at all. The unfinished business ran on into the Thirty Years' War.

Paul III approves Ignatius of Loyola's small company of graduates as a religious order under a fourth vow of obedience to the pope. Mobile where monks were settled, and schoolmasters by instinct, the Jesuits became the sharp edge of the Catholic Reformation and its most far-flung missionaries — Xavier to India and Japan, Ricci to China.

The most learned and least easy-going of the Latin fathers, who went to Bethlehem, learned Hebrew, and translated the Scriptures from the original tongues into the Latin the West would read for a thousand years. His insistence on the Hebrew canon over the wider Greek collection set up the argument with Augustine that the Reformation would reopen. See the vault's [[Jerome]] note.

At Kettering, twelve Particular Baptist ministers — William Carey among them — found a mission society with a collection of thirteen pounds, putting Carey's 'Expect great things from God; attempt great things for God' into practice and opening the modern missionary movement.
Commemoration of the merchant's son who embraced poverty to follow Christ, founded the Franciscan order, and preached the gospel to rich, poor and creation alike.

Strangled and burned at Vilvoorde near Brussels for the crime of putting the Bible into English from the Greek and Hebrew. His last recorded prayer was that God would open the king of England's eyes — and within four years an English Bible built largely on his own work was licensed for every parish church. Much of its wording is still in the ear of anyone who reads the King James Version. See the vault's [[Tyndale's New Testament]] note.
The fourth ecumenical council defines that Christ is one person in two natures, fully God and fully man — the touchstone of orthodox Christology.
Pope John XXIII opens the twenty-first ecumenical council, whose reforms — vernacular liturgy, ecumenical outreach — reshaped the modern Roman Catholic Church.
Latimer and Ridley martyred at Oxford
Bishops Hugh Latimer and Nicholas Ridley are burned under Mary I. Latimer's words to Ridley endured: a candle lit in England that would never be put out.

Bishop of Antioch, taken under guard to Rome to die in the arena. On the road he wrote seven letters to the churches — begging them not to save him, urging them to hold to their bishops, and giving us the earliest surviving use of the phrase 'the catholic church'. He is the clearest window we have into the church one generation after the apostles.

The treaties signed at Münster and Osnabrück end the Thirty Years' War, which had killed perhaps a third of the German population over religion and power. Augsburg's settlement is extended to the Reformed, and Europe's rulers effectively give up on reuniting Christendom by force. The wars of religion end — not in agreement, but in exhaustion.

By tradition Martin Luther posts his theses against the sale of indulgences on the Castle Church door in Wittenberg — the spark of the Protestant Reformation. See the vault's [[Protestant Reformation]] note.

Nearly a hundred South African denominations — including churches that had defended apartheid and churches that had suffered under it — meet at Rustenburg as the country begins to change. The Dutch Reformed theologian Willie Jonker confessed his church's guilt from the floor and Desmond Tutu answered him; the conference's declaration bound the signatories to restitution, not words only.

Commemoration of the soldier who, converted, shared his cloak with a beggar and became bishop of Tours — one of the first non-martyrs the church honoured as a saint. His feast, Martinmas, long marked the start of winter.
On Martinmas the Fourth Lateran Council opens under Innocent III — the largest council the medieval West had seen, defining transubstantiation and requiring annual confession.

Aboard ship off Cape Cod, the Pilgrims covenant themselves into a 'civil body politic' — the congregational church covenant applied to civil order. Signed 11 November by the old calendar, 21 November by the new.

Commemoration of the Oxford don, apologist and storyteller — Mere Christianity, the Chronicles of Narnia — who died this day in 1963, an hour before the world's eyes turned to Dallas. Kept in the American Episcopal calendar.
Urban II preaches the First Crusade

At Clermont, Urban II summons the knighthood of Europe to the aid of the Eastern churches and the recovery of Jerusalem — 'Deus vult.' The crusades that followed left a legacy the church still reckons with.
Commemoration of the fourth-century bishop famed for secret generosity — the historical root of Father Christmas — and, by tradition, a defender of Nicene orthodoxy.

A provincial governor acclaimed bishop by the crowd while he was still unbaptized, who gave away his property and set about learning theology in public. He taught the West to sing hymns, faced down an emperor over a massacre and made him do penance, and his preaching is what finally broke Augustine's resistance.

Weeks after Sharpeville, the World Council of Churches convenes South African member churches at Cottesloe in Johannesburg. The delegates — Dutch Reformed among them — rejected the scriptural case for apartheid. Verwoerd applied pressure, the Afrikaans churches withdrew their assent, and Beyers Naudé's refusal to withdraw his cost him his pulpit.
At Wittenberg's Elster Gate, Luther publicly burns the bull Exsurge Domine and volumes of canon law — a point of no return in the break with Rome.
The Roman Catholic Church's answer to the Reformation begins its long series of sessions, defining doctrine and reforming abuses. See the vault's [[Council of Trent (1546)]] note.
On Christmas Day in St Peter's, Leo III crowns Charlemagne emperor — binding church and empire in the arrangement that would define, and haunt, Western Christendom for a thousand years.
The Archbishop of Canterbury is cut down in his own cathedral by knights of Henry II after a long struggle over the church's liberties — Europe's most famous medieval martyrdom.
Commemoration of the Oxford 'Morning Star of the Reformation,' who taught the supreme authority of Scripture and inspired the first complete English Bible; he died this day in 1384.
